title: Nvidia tells cloud resellers that 51 percent of capacity must go to non-Chinese clients and halves its Asian buyer whitelist
subtitle: The rules were communicated verbally rather than in written contracts, according to Financial Times reporting, and tighten what Southeast Asian neoclouds can do with the GPUs they already have.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Nvidia has told cloud-reselling customers that at least 51 percent of their capacity must be rented to non-Chinese firms, according to Financial Times reporting picked up by DatacenterDynamics. The instruction was reportedly delivered verbally rather than in written contracts, so it does not appear in the public distributor agreements. In parallel, Nvidia has cut its list of authorized buyers of its most advanced equipment in Asia by more than half, dropping customers in Singapore, Malaysia and Japan from the whitelist and layering on on-site inspections and end-user reviews for those that remain.

The two changes close different gaps in the same wall. The 51 percent rule limits what a Southeast Asian neocloud can do with GPUs it already owns, since a provider that rents past that threshold to Chinese-headquartered firms loses its ability to buy more. The whitelist cut addresses the upstream side, narrowing who can purchase Nvidia's top SKUs in the first place. Together they push much of the US export regime into private contract terms, where the enforcement mechanism is not a federal subpoena but the credible threat of being cut off by the manufacturer.

Pushback is already surfacing. Singapore neocloud groups told the Financial Times that it is hard to find enough non-Chinese demand outside the US to fill the gap. A separate strand of this story is the US Commerce Department's interim final rule requiring export licenses for shipments to foreign data centers above 12 million total processing performance, roughly 750 H100 or H200 chips. Nvidia is playing both sides of that fence: tightening the private rules fast enough that the public rule, when it bites, finds less to catch — and keeping its enterprise customers inside the fence even while Beijing holds back some shipments after Washington approvals.

A note for learners: in regulated industries, the clauses that matter are often the ones outside the contract. A verbal rule a vendor can revoke with a phone call is harder to challenge in court than a written clause, and harder to copy for compliance programs. If you are building anything that depends on GPU access — a startup, a research cluster, a student project at an institution with overseas partners — get the actual terms in writing from your reseller, including what triggers a loss of supply. The rules will keep changing; your audit trail is what protects you.
